content:
A favourite challenge: the Quran calls itself clear and detailed, so show the five daily prayers (salah) from the Quran alone. If you cannot, the book is not detailed after all.

The challenge assumes Islam was meant to run on the Quran alone. The Quran itself says otherwise. The entries below set out what the Quran gives on the times of prayer, where it sends readers for the rest, what its claim to detail means, how the five prayers were handed down, and what happens when the same test is turned on the New Testament.

The challenge is worth taking seriously because it comes from two directions. Some critics use it to argue that the Quran is incomplete, and a small number of Muslims, often called Quranists, use it to argue that the hadith should be set aside and the Quran read alone. Both rest on the same assumption about how the Quran presents itself, and the Quran's own verses are the place to test it.

It tells believers to establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night.[1] It points to prayer from the sun's decline to the darkness of night, and the recitation at dawn.[2] It speaks of glorifying God before sunrise and before sunset, and in the hours of the night.[3]

Another passage calls for glorifying God in the evening, in the morning, in the afternoon and at noon, and elsewhere the Quran says that prayer is prescribed for believers at fixed times.[4] Dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset and night can all be read out of these scattered verses, and the classical jurists drew the five from them together with the practice they had seen.

The times are there. The count and the form come from somewhere else, and the Quran says where.

The Quran gives more than the times. It names the dawn prayer and the night prayer, salat al-fajr and salat al-isha, as times of privacy in the household, and it tells believers to guard the prayers and "the middle prayer".[5] A report in al-Bukhari and Muslim identifies the middle prayer as the afternoon prayer, which the Prophet said his enemies had kept him from on the day of the Trench.[6] The Quran also describes the actions of prayer, standing, bowing and prostrating, sets out the washing that precedes it, allows it to be shortened on a journey, and describes how it is to be prayed in danger, with one group standing guard while another prays.[7]

A reader who collects those verses finds a great deal of the form of the prayer in the Quran itself. What it does not give is a step-by-step manual, and the next entry explains why it did not need to.

It tells believers to obey God and obey the Messenger,[8] and to take what the Messenger gives and refrain from what he forbids.[9] It describes him as the one who explains to people what was sent down to them.[10] It calls his conduct a good example for those who hope in God and the Last Day.[11]

A book that tells you to follow a teacher for the detail has told you where the detail lives.

The Quran treats other duties the same way. It commands zakah, the annual giving, many times without stating the rates, and the pilgrimage (hajj) without setting out its rites. Nobody has been able to follow those commands without the Prophet's teaching. The jurists, al-Shafii among them, argued from these verses that the Prophet's explanation is part of how the Quran is meant to be read.

Ismail al Faruqi puts the relation in a single phrase: the Prophet's practice (sunnah, "trodden path") supplies "the exemplary 'how' for the 'what' of revelation", and from it Muslims take the whole form of their worship.[12]

The Prophet put the principle in a short instruction. A group of young men stayed with him for twenty days to learn the religion, and when they left he told them: "Pray as you have seen me praying."[13] The form of the prayer was taught by being shown, and the community that watched him pray passed it on by praying.

When the Quran calls itself a detailed explanation of all things, the classical reading is that it sets out everything needed for guidance, directly or by pointing to its source.[14] It never claims to be a liturgical rubric. The critic's reading makes "detailed" mean something no Muslim scholar ever took it to mean.

The strongest form of the objection quotes a second verse: God has neglected nothing in the Book.[15] Commentators differ on whether "the Book" there means the Quran or God's whole record of creation. On the first reading the verse still includes the command to obey the Messenger, which is how the detail of prayer reaches the reader. A modern movement that holds to the Quran alone does exist. It has to explain away the verses of the previous entry and the unbroken practice described in the next.

The modern movement has a history. In the late nineteenth century, groups in Punjab calling themselves Ahl al-Quran, the people of the Quran, tried to derive the whole of practice from the Quran alone, and in the twentieth century Ghulam Ahmad Parwez argued a related case in Pakistan.[16] Their own experience illustrates the difficulty. Without the Prophet's practice, Quranist groups have reached different answers on the number of daily prayers and on how to perform them. The disagreement among them shows what the Quran's instruction to follow the Messenger was meant to prevent.

The five daily prayers are among the most widely transmitted practices in Islam, performed publicly, in congregation, five times a day, from the first generation to now. No early Muslim community prayed three, and none prayed seven.

A practice performed billions of times, in every Muslim city, since the 7th century, is known the way public practice is always known: people watched it, and joined in.

The hadith (reports of the Prophet's words and deeds) record how it began. In a well-known report a man from the desert asked what God had made obligatory on him in prayer, and the Prophet answered with the five prayers of the day and night.[17] Other reports describe Gabriel leading the Prophet through the times of prayer,[18] and the night journey, after which fifty prayers were reduced to five.[19] A sceptic may question any single report. The practice does not rest on a single report.

Muslim scholars called knowledge of this kind tawatur: a fact transmitted by so many people, in so many places, that their agreement on a falsehood is inconceivable. The number of prayers, the number of units in each, the call to prayer and the facing of Mecca all belong to it. A sceptic who doubts every report about the Prophet still has to explain how every Muslim community, from Spain to Central Asia within a century of his death, came to pray the same five prayers in the same way.

The strongest form of the objection is that a practice can drift as it spreads, so uniformity proves only that a later authority imposed it. The answer is that no authority in early Islam had the power to impose a single form of daily worship on a community that stretched across three continents and disagreed fiercely on politics. The schools of law that grew up in that community disagree on many details of prayer. They agree on the five.

Ask a Christian to prove the Trinity, infant baptism or Sunday worship from the text alone, with no church tradition. Every Christian community relies on received practice to read its scripture.

The New Testament does describe the first Christians meeting on the first day of the week,[20] but it gives no command to hold the Sabbath on Sunday. Christians who hold that scripture alone is the final authority still rely on early creeds to state the Trinity, and on the church's decisions in the early centuries to fix the list of books that make up the New Testament. The point is not that these practices lack defenders. Each is defended from tradition as well as text.

Early Christian practice confirms the point from outside the New Testament. The Didache, a church manual from around the end of the first century, tells Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day.[21] No verse of the New Testament sets that rule. Jewish practice works the same way: the three daily prayers are drawn from the example of Daniel and the patriarchs, and fixed by the rabbis in the Talmud.[22] Fixed daily prayer in all three faiths rests on scripture read through a living practice.

That is how revealed religion has always worked in both faiths: a text, and the people who lived it.

The bottom line

The Quran gives the times of prayer, commands obedience to the Prophet, and leaves the form to him. The Prophet prayed five times a day in public, and his community has done the same ever since. The same pattern holds for zakah and the hajj, where the Quran gives the command and the Prophet's practice gives the detail.

The challenge only works for someone who has decided in advance that Islam must be Quran-only. Islam never has been. A person can still hold that scripture alone should settle every question, and that view has defenders in Christianity as well. It cannot be derived from the Quran, which points elsewhere, and it has no early Muslim community behind it.

The deeper answer is about what a revealed book is for. The Quran calls itself guidance and a reminder, and it gives its hearers a teacher who lived among them. A book that tried to replace that teacher with a manual would have had to anticipate every question of practice in advance. A book that sends its readers to a living example, preserved by the community that followed it, leaves the detail where it can be seen and learned.
